title: -ing and -ed adjectives: causes and feelings
summary: Distinguish qualities that produce a reaction from the feelings that people experience. Use -ing adjectives for interesting, tiring or surprising experiences and -ed adjectives for how people feel in response, with natural complements.
learningObjectives: Use -ing adjectives to describe events, activities or people that produce a feeling.
Use -ed adjectives to describe someone experiencing a feeling or reaction.
Distinguish pairs such as confusing/confused and frightening/frightened in realistic contexts.
Use expressions such as interested in, excited about and disappointed with naturally.

explanation.heading: Use -ing to describe what causes a feeling
explanation.body: Many -ing adjectives describe a quality of an experience, thing or person that creates a reaction. A confusing notice causes confusion; an entertaining performance makes people enjoy themselves. The -ing ending is part of the adjective here, not necessarily a present continuous verb.
explanation.example: The instructions were confusing, so we asked for an example.

explanation.heading: Use -ed to describe a person’s reaction
explanation.body: An -ed adjective usually tells us how somebody feels because of an event or experience. The same event may be disappointing while its audience feels disappointed. Do not use an -ing adjective for the person’s feeling unless you actually mean that the person causes that reaction in others.
explanation.example: The audience was disappointed by the cancelled concert.

explanation.heading: A person can be interesting or interested
explanation.body: The choice depends on meaning, not simply whether the subject is human. An interesting speaker keeps an audience engaged; an interested speaker wants to learn more about a subject. Similarly, a boring person makes others bored, while a bored person is experiencing boredom.
explanation.example: The guide was interesting, and the visitors were interested in her stories.

explanation.heading: Match common adjective pairs to context
explanation.body: Common pairs include exciting/excited, tiring/tired, exhausting/exhausted, surprising/surprised, frightening/frightened, embarrassing/embarrassed and satisfying/satisfied. Choose the adjective by deciding whether the noun or person is the source of the feeling or the person experiencing it.
explanation.example: The sudden announcement was surprising, and the staff were surprised.

explanation.heading: Use natural complements with feeling adjectives
explanation.body: Some -ed adjectives commonly combine with prepositions: interested in a subject, excited about a plan, disappointed with or by a result, and frightened of or by something. The preposition links the feeling to its topic or cause. Get + an -ed adjective often describes the moment a feeling develops.
explanation.example: Maya got excited about the chance to study abroad.

left.label: -ing: the cause
left.note: The workshop demanded so much effort that it made people very tired.

right.label: -ed: the reaction
right.note: The people felt the result of the demanding workshop.

comparisons.title: Person who causes interest versus person who feels it

left.label: Interesting
left.note: Ravi makes other people interested in his stories.

right.label: Interested
right.example: Ravi is interested in local history.
right.note: Ravi himself feels curiosity about the subject.

examples.sentence: The documentary was fascinating, and several viewers asked questions afterward.
examples.note: Fascinating describes the film as something that attracts interest.

examples.sentence: Everyone was confused by the new timetable.
examples.note: Confused tells us the reaction of the people, not the quality of the timetable.

examples.sentence: It was an embarrassing mistake, but she did not stay embarrassed for long.
examples.note: Embarrassing characterises the mistake, while embarrassed describes her feeling.

examples.sentence: Our first flight was frightening because of strong winds.
examples.note: Frightening describes the journey as a cause of fear.

examples.sentence: The research team was satisfied with the results of the trial.
examples.note: Satisfied describes the team’s reaction, with with connecting it to the results.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I was confusing when I read the timetable.
commonMistakes.correct: I was confused when I read the timetable.
commonMistakes.why: Confused describes the reader’s feeling; confusing would mean the person caused confusion in others.
The journey caused fatigue; exhausted is normally a description of a tired person.

commonMistakes.incorrect: She is interesting in joining the book club.
commonMistakes.correct: She is interested in joining the book club.
commonMistakes.why: Interested in describes her desire to join, not her effect on other people.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The children were frightening by the sudden noise.
commonMistakes.correct: The children were frightened by the sudden noise.
commonMistakes.why: The children experienced fear, so use frightened; frightening would describe a cause of fear.

studyTips: For each adjective pair, write two linked sentences: the situation was confusing; the people were confused.
When the subject is a person, check the meaning: are they causing a reaction in others or feeling that reaction themselves?
Learn frequently used combinations as chunks: interested in, excited about, disappointed with and frightened by.

exercises.prompt: The instructions were so ___ that nobody knew which form to complete.
exercises.feedback: The instructions caused confusion, so confusing describes their effect on readers.

exercises.prompt: After the overnight journey, everyone felt ___.
exercises.feedback: Exhausted describes how the travellers felt after a tiring experience.

exercises.prompt: Lena tells wonderful stories. She is a very ___ person to listen to.
exercises.feedback: Interesting describes Lena as someone who holds other people’s attention.

exercises.prompt: The final result was ___, so the players looked ___.
exercises.feedback: The result caused the reaction, so it was surprising; the players felt surprised.

exercises.prompt: The trainees felt ___ by the unclear diagram. (confuse; use the adjective for a feeling)
exercises.feedback: Confused describes the trainees’ reaction to a diagram they could not understand.

exercises.prompt: The dance performance was ___. (amaze; use the adjective describing its effect)
exercises.feedback: Amazing describes a performance that caused wonder in its audience.

exercises.prompt: I felt ___ when I forgot the presenter’s name. (embarrass; use the feeling adjective)
exercises.feedback: Embarrassed describes how the speaker felt after making the mistake.

exercises.prompt: Travelling to the remote village was ___, although the visit was worth it. (tire; describe the journey)
exercises.feedback: The journey made people tired, so tiring describes the cause.

exercises.prompt: Correct by changing only the adjective: I was very surprising when the decision was announced.
acceptedAnswers: I was very surprised when the decision was announced.
exercises.feedback: Surprised describes the speaker’s feeling after hearing the decision.

exercises.prompt: Correct by changing only the adjective: The lecture was so bored that several people left early.
acceptedAnswers: The lecture was so boring that several people left early.
exercises.feedback: The lecture made listeners bored; boring describes the cause.

exercises.prompt: Correct by changing only the adjective: We are interesting in taking the afternoon class.
acceptedAnswers: We are interested in taking the afternoon class.
exercises.feedback: Interested in expresses the group’s desire to join the class.

exercises.prompt: Correct by changing only the adjective: The sudden loud noise was frightened for the young visitors.
acceptedAnswers: The sudden loud noise was frightening for the young visitors.
exercises.feedback: Frightening describes the noise as a cause of fear, not as someone who feels afraid.

speakingExercises.prompt: A new project makes the team feel excited. Describe the project as the cause. Begin “The new project” and use exciting.
speakingExercises.feedback: Exciting identifies the project as something that creates excitement.

speakingExercises.prompt: You feel excitement about the new project. Say one sentence starting “I am” and ending “about the new project”. Use excited.
acceptedAnswers: I am excited about the new project.
I'm excited about the new project.
speakingExercises.feedback: Excited describes the speaker’s feeling, followed by about to name its cause.

speakingExercises.prompt: The instructions caused confusion in the team. Produce exactly two sentences. First begin “The instructions were”; second begin “The team was”. Use confusing and confused.
acceptedAnswers: The instructions were confusing. The team was confused.
speakingExercises.feedback: The source of confusion is confusing; the people experiencing it are confused.

speakingExercises.prompt: A long course made Dana extremely tired. Describe the course, not Dana. Begin “The course” and use exhausting.
speakingExercises.feedback: Exhausting describes the course as the cause of fatigue.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct only the adjective, then say the full sentence: “The result was surprised.”
speakingExercises.feedback: The result causes surprise; it does not experience the feeling.

speakingExercises.prompt: A museum guide tells stories that hold everyone’s attention. Describe the guide in a complete sentence. Start “The guide” and use interesting.
speakingExercises.feedback: A person can be interesting when they cause interest in other people.

speakingExercises.prompt: Paraphrase the supplied fact as a feeling: “The long delay annoyed us.” Begin “We were” and finish “by the long delay”.
acceptedAnswers: We were annoyed by the long delay.
speakingExercises.feedback: Annoyed describes the group’s reaction; by names the cause.

speakingExercises.prompt: Produce exactly two sentences about these facts. First: the loud noise caused fear; use “The noise was frightening.” Second: the children felt fear; use “The children were frightened.”
acceptedAnswers: The noise was frightening. The children were frightened.
speakingExercises.feedback: Frightening describes the cause; frightened describes the children’s feeling.

listeningExercises.audioText: I expected the presentation to be dull, but it was fascinating. I left feeling inspired.
listeningExercises.prompt: How did the speaker feel after the presentation?
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker found the presentation fascinating and explicitly says they felt inspired.

listeningExercises.audioText: The instructions were confusing, so the new volunteers asked for a practical demonstration.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why did the volunteers ask for a demonstration?
choices: The instructions were difficult to understand.
They already knew the procedure perfectly.
listeningExercises.feedback: Confusing explains why the volunteers needed an additional demonstration.

listeningExercises.audioText: The long walk uphill was exhausting, even though the view was beautiful.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single adjective immediately after “was” in the recording.
listeningExercises.feedback: Exhausting describes the walk as something that caused tiredness.

listeningExercises.audioText: Marco tells amusing stories at dinner, but he looked bored during the long speech.
choices: He makes others laugh, but the speech did not interest him.
He was frightened by his own stories.
He was entertaining the audience throughout the speech.
listeningExercises.feedback: Amusing describes his usual stories; bored describes his reaction to the speech.

listeningExercises.audioText: The race results were disappointing. We had hoped to finish first, but our team came fourth.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why did the team feel disappointed?
choices: They won by a narrow margin.
They did not finish as high as they had hoped.
The race was cancelled before the finish.
listeningExercises.feedback: The team expected first place but came fourth; disappointing refers to that outcome.

listeningExercises.audioText: The science exhibit was frightening for the younger children, but the adults found it interesting.
listeningExercises.prompt: How did the two groups respond differently?
choices: The adults were frightened and the children were interested.
The children felt afraid, while the adults were interested.
listeningExercises.feedback: Frightening describes the effect on children, while interesting describes the adults’ reaction.

listeningExercises.audioText: At first I was embarrassed by my mistake, but everyone was kind about it.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single adjective immediately after “was” in the recording.
listeningExercises.feedback: Embarrassed describes the speaker’s own reaction to making the mistake.

listeningExercises.audioText: The documentary was inspiring, and the students felt inspired after watching it.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single adjective immediately after “felt” in the recording.
listeningExercises.feedback: Inspired describes the students’ reaction to the inspiring documentary.
